# Getting started

## Why are we here

-   Quantitative analysis skills important (in academia and beyond)
-   Many courses teach statistics, few teach how to do the programming
-   Manual copying of data/ results always (!) error prone

## Introduction to course

-   I am only a facilitator
-   You decide what you take from it
-   Idea is to work continuously on project

## Learning goals of the course

-   Learning some R
-   Apply what you know in real research project
-   Empower you to continue on your journey

## Learning goals of today

-   Introduction (you, me, course)
-   Setting expectations
-   Setting up R, Quarto and Github

## Assessment

-   Progress report (Every two weeks Friday at 15:00)
-   Final script of project

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### 3 Credit Points (CP)

-   Short presentation (10 minutes)
-   Short final research note with references (\~5 pages, at least one high-quality graph)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### 6 Credit Points (CP)

-   Long presentation (20 minutes)
-   Long final research note with references (\~10 pages, at least two high-quality graphs)
:::
:::::

## Assessment - Progress report

-   Simple progress report, free form (one short paragraph)
-   I tried setting it up on StudIP, might change
-   I expect 5 short reports:
-   one can be dropped without explanation
-   after that need a good excuse

## Assessment - Script (each 25%)

-   Correct: Is the script correct and does what it should?
-   Structure: Is the structure helpful and appropriate?
-   Clarity: Does it become clear what the script does and when?
- Comments: Are the comments in the script enough to follow it?

## Assessment - Presentation criteria (each 25%)

-   Structure: Is the structure helpful and appropriate?
-   Clarity: Does it become clear what you present on?
-   Visuals: Does the presentation look appealing?
-   Presentation: Are you presenting convincingly?

## Assessment - Research note criteria (each 25%)

-   Structure: Is the structure helpful and appropriate?
-   Clarity: Does it become clear what you are writing on?
-   Visuals: Does the data sicualisation look appealing?
-   References: Are the references correct and relevant?

# Installing R

## Why R?

::::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Pro

-   free
-   open source
-   large community
-   innovative
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
### Contra

-   steeper learning curve
-   many ways to achieve the same goal
-   No authoratative singular guide online
:::
:::::

## Why RStudio?

-   If you use R, one should use RStudio
-   provides a clearer interface
-   Adds features that make programming easier
-   Unfortunately, proprietary (but for free)

## Installing R and RStudio

-   Download R here: https://cran.r-project.org/mirrors.html
-   Download RStudio here: https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop

# Installing Quarto

## Why Quarto?

-   Quarto is a programme to write technical documents
-   Same (for R-users) as RMarkdown
-   Seamless integrates (R-)code and text with references (Zotero)
-   Outputs PDFs, but also HTML (and other formats)

## Do you need to use Quarto?

-   No, but it is highly encouraged
-   We will be working in R
-   Adding Quarto costs little extra effort but adds a lot
-   Very good explanatory resources here: https://quarto.org/docs/guide/

## Installing Quarto

-   You can download Quarto here: https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/

# git

## Why git?

-   git is a distributed version control software system
-   Allows to save and track progress in the cloud
-   Enables collaboration on code with a team
-   There are a range of providers for git (e.g. www.github.com)

## Do you need to use git?

-   No, but it is encouraged
-   It costs a little bit of time to set up
-   but once set-up, it acts as a safety net for your code

## Installing and setting up git

-   Great explainer on how to integrate git in R: https://happygitwithr.com/
-   another explainer: https://rfortherestofus.com/2021/02/how-to-use-git-github-with-r/
